name: codezen
summary: Skills for building software, from Korza.
problem: Agent-assisted work tends to jump straight to code. Requirements stay half-specified, and tests become an afterthought.
benefits: Covers requirements, build and test, so the work either side of writing code is part of the process.
Korza's own plugin, so the conventions it applies are the ones your reviewers already expect.

name: pyright-lsp
summary: Listed in the catalogue; ships nothing today.
problem: Without a language server the agent reads Python as plain text. It infers signatures instead of looking them up, and type errors an IDE would flag immediately go unnoticed.
benefits: Does not currently work. The installed plugin directory contains no skill, agent, hook or LSP-server definitions, because the entry keeps its lspServers configuration outside that directory and the catalogue copies only the directory.
Intended to give the agent real diagnostics and type information on Python code, which is what it will do once the entry is repaired or replaced.
Tracked as a known defect rather than a recommendation: install it only to reproduce the problem.

name: superpowers
summary: Core skills library: TDD, debugging, collaboration.
problem: Left to itself, an agent writes code first and reasons about it afterwards. The result reads well and fails under test.
benefits: A vetted library of TDD, debugging and collaboration patterns, so the approach is not improvised on every task.
Pinned to a tag rather than a branch, so upstream commits cannot land on your machine unreviewed. The trade is that the pin has to be moved deliberately, and it is currently one release behind.
codezen builds on it, so the two are designed to run together.

name: mattpocock-skills
summary: Matt Pocock's engineering and productivity skills.
problem: The jobs around writing code get re-improvised every time: reviewing a PR, diagnosing a bug, turning a spec into tickets, handing work over. How well they go depends on who asked and how.
benefits: Twenty-five task-specific skills covering review, TDD, domain modelling, triage and architecture.
Includes the communication side of the work: teaching, handoffs, questionnaires, writing for agents.
Currently tracks main rather than a tag, so upstream commits reach your machine unreviewed. v1.2.3 declares the same twenty-five skills, so there is nothing blocking a pin.

name: humanizer
summary: Removes the signs of AI-generated writing from text.
problem: AI prose has tells: inflated symbolism, promotional language, em dash overuse, the rule of three, filler phrases. Readers notice them even when they cannot name them.
benefits: Edits against Wikipedia's documented "Signs of AI writing" list rather than a vague sense of tone.
Worth running on anything customer-facing: docs, release notes, incident writeups.
Small enough to read end to end before you trust it: one skill, and the whole prompt is in the repository.
